A $2.2 Billion Fund Just Bought These 3 Stocks ©bluebay2014 from Getty Images and Africa images from Canva
Key Takeaways

Discovery Capital Management's latest 13F shows its three biggest new or added positions in the third quarter were Amazon, Take-Two Interactive and First Solar.

Analysts' average targets sit 32% to 82% above the last close for all three.

Amazon's faster cloud growth and rising targets back the fund's biggest add, while First Solar's guidance cut makes its gap harder to trust.

Of the three, Amazon has the strongest case on the numbers.

A $2.2 billion fund just put fresh money into three very different stocks: Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ), Take-Two Interactive (TTWO:NASDAQ) and First Solar (FSLR:NASDAQ). Discovery Capital Management's 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed Nov. 16, shows them as its three biggest new or added positions. (That $2.2 billion is what its 13F holds in US stocks: $2.18 billion across 102 positions.)

Amazon is now a top-three holding

Discovery held 456,739 Amazon shares at Sept. 30, 159% more than the quarter before. They were worth $114 million, or 5.2% of its 13F, its No. 3 position, and the stock is down 0.9% since the quarter's end.

Amazon gave the bet plenty of support in its third-quarter report on Oct. 29. AWS sales grew 39% to $46.0 billion, up from 37% growth in the second quarter, and GAAP operating income of $28.1 billion made for a 13.9% operating margin, Amazon's highest ever.

The catch is the cash. CEO Andy Jassy said on CNBC on Nov. 17 that Amazon will spend about $220 billion this year and "meaningfully more" in 2027. Consensus has free cash flow at a $41.2 billion outflow in 2026 before a $35.7 billion inflow in 2028.

Analysts have kept raising their targets anyway. The consensus target rose to $327 from $294 a year ago, 32% above the last close:

Amazon.com (AMZN): analysts' consensus (mean) price target, $ per share, last year (TIKR)

And at about 25x forward earnings, Amazon trades below its one-year average of about 30x on TIKR, even though analysts raised their 2028 earnings estimates 24% over the year to Oct. 23.

TIKR tracks 62 analysts on Amazon. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Amazon, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Amazon's Analyst Ratings

Take-Two finally has its blockbuster

Take-Two is a smaller bet. Discovery added 91% to its stake, ending the quarter with 219,100 shares worth $45 million, 2.1% of its 13F and its No. 11 holding. The stock is up 1% since Sept. 30.

The case is Grand Theft Auto VI, which launched Nov. 19. Take-Two said the game brought in an estimated $3.79 billion of retail sales on its first day, the biggest entertainment launch ever by its count. (That's what shoppers spent, and Take-Two keeps only part of it.)

Key Takeaways

Cathie Wood's ARK Invest sold 37,002 shares of Amazon from its ARK Innovation ETF on Friday, worth about $9 million at the day's close.

The sale is small next to the 1.70 million Amazon shares ARK held at the end of September.

Analysts expect Amazon's earnings to nearly double from 2025 to 2028, and the stock trades at 24x forward earnings, half its five-year average.

Amazon's AI spending and its Anthropic stake, which now has a public price, are the risks, but at this multiple the numbers favor buying over selling.

Cathie Wood's ARK Invest sold 37,002 shares of Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ) on Friday, according to ARK's daily trade email. At Friday's close of $246.82, that comes to about $9 million. That figure is the shares times the close, since ARK doesn't say what it got for them.

It was a rough day to trade anything in tech. The Nasdaq 100 fell 6% on Friday, the day after Anthropic (ANT:NASDAQ) went public. Anthropic's latest amended S-1 puts Amazon's stake at 14.7% after the offering.

A small trim from ARK's flagship fund

All 37,002 shares came out of the ARK Innovation ETF (ARKK), where they made up 0.06% of the fund. That's a small move, and it's also small next to what ARK owned going in.

ARK manages $17 billion. Its 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed Nov. 13, showed 1.70 million Amazon shares worth $423 million. That's 2.4% of its 13F stocks and its 13th-largest holding. ARK also held 7% more Amazon shares on Sept. 30 than it did three months earlier, so Friday's sale trims a stake that grew last quarter.

title: 2 Growth Stocks That Could Double by 2031
detail:
2 Growth Stocks That Could Double by 2031
John Ballard, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 21, 2026 at 1:25 PM CST 4 min read
NVDA
AMZN
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Sticking with familiar brands and services is one of the best ways for the average investor to pick winning stocks. A stock's price tends to follow its earnings over time. A company growing earnings at least 15% a year can double in five years, and some of the most dominant consumer services can still achieve that level of growth.

Wall Street expects the following top growth stocks to deliver 19% or better annual earnings growth, putting a double by 2031 within reach.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Amazon

Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN)shares closed at $257.89 on Nov. 17, up 11% over the past year and 45% over the past five years, trailing the S&P 500's 56% five-year return. The reason it can double by 2031 is expanding margins, which the market hasn't fully priced in yet.

Over the past three years, Amazon's trailing-12-month operating income has risen 283% to $106 billion. Amazon's most profitable business is its cloud services segment. Still, it has many levers to increase profitability from growth in other non-retail services, which make up the majority of its $797 billion in annual revenue.

Advertising is a profitable business to watch. Amazon sells ads to brands and sellers that want to reach its shoppers. Ad revenue grew 12% year over year on a constant-currency basis to $19.6 billion in the third quarter, bringing it close to $80 billion annually.

However, that growth doesn't show the real momentum. Moving Prime Day into Q2 cut 8.5 percentage points from Q3 ad growth, according to CEO Andy Jassy. Excluding currency swings, ad sales grew 22% to 26% in each of the five prior quarters, and management expects ad growth to return to the high teens in Q4.

Amazon trades at about 27 times forward earnings, which is reasonable given analysts' expectations that earnings will grow about 24% per year over the coming years. If the valuation multiple holds, and Amazon delivers on those expectations, the stock could more than double by 2031.

Airbnb

Airbnb (NASDAQ:ABNB)shares closed at $180.94 on Nov. 17, up 54% over the past year but down 9% over the past five years. The business has continued to grow, creating a good buying opportunity.

Management says "Airbnb is back in growth mode." Q3 revenue rose 19% year over year, its fastest growth in more than three years, and management raised its full-year outlook.

Microsoft nearly doubled its capital spending in the year to June 2026. Capital spending is money put into long-lived assets, such as data centers. Even so, Microsoft had cash left over.

Friday, Nov 20, was a hard day for AI stocks. Nvidia fell 14.0%, a chip-stock fund (SMH) 10.6% and the Nasdaq 100 fund (QQQ) 5.7%. Microsoft fell 2.8%, less than the S&P 500 fund (SPY), which lost 3.6%.

Source: Microsoft's cash-flow statements, fiscal years ending June 30. "Left over" is cash brought in minus capital spending, buybacks and dividends. A negative "borrowed" means it repaid more debt than it took on.

Microsoft's capital spending reached $116 billion in its last fiscal year, up from $65 billion. It still paid shareholders nearly $49 billion. It also paid down $3 billion of debt. Every other big AI buyer borrowed in the year to September. Microsoft repaid. Then, on Nov. 4, it sold $25 billion of new bonds.

Its interest bill last fiscal year was $3.1 billion. That was less than the $3.3 billion it earned on its cash. The latest quarter, to September, shows the pace rising. Microsoft spent $39.4 billion against $58.0 billion brought in. We follow the other big builders' cash in Big Tech Earned $607 Billion. Where Did It Go?

Microsoft nearly doubled its capital spending and still paid its shareholders nearly $49 billion. If you want your savings to pay you an income, that kind of cash is what to look for. Yes, about $39 billion more from its own cash.

Analysts expect sales of $396 billion in the year to June 2027, or fiscal 2027. Microsoft turns about 57 cents of every $1 of sales into cash. On those sales, that is about $224 billion.

title: Buy Microsoft and Amazon at More Than 70x 2028 Free Cash Flow? Here’s What Their Capex Must Return

Buy Microsoft and Amazon at More Than 70x 2028 Free Cash Flow? Here's What Their Capex Must Return ©jiefeng jiang from Getty Images and Quality Stock Arts via Canva
Key Takeaways

At the Nov. 20 close, Microsoft traded at about 77x the free cash flow analysts expect for fiscal 2028, and Amazon traded at about 75x.

Amazon plans to spend about $220 billion on capex this year and more next year, and analysts expect its free cash flow to stay negative until 2028.

At 30x free cash flow, both would need far more cash than they've ever made, and the capex peak that gets them there could slow Arista Networks.

Microsoft's contracted backlog makes its bet easier to trust than Amazon's.

Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ) CEO Andy Jassy has no plans to slow down. Asked on CNBC's Halftime Report on Nov. 17 about Wall Street's capex forecasts, he said "we expect to spend around $220 billion this year in CapEx and that we expect to spend meaningfully more next year."

A lot of that money becomes revenue for suppliers like Arista Networks (ANET:NYSE).

One investor in r/ValueInvesting argued that Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ) and Amazon trade at more than 80 times estimated fiscal 2028 free cash flow.

TIKR's estimates backed that up at the Nov. 18 close. Then two days of tech selling took about 5% off Microsoft and 8% off Amazon. Both now trade below 80x, but still above 70x.

Still More Than 70x

At the Nov. 20 close, Microsoft was worth about $3.60 trillion, or about 77x the $46.8 billion of free cash flow analysts expect in its fiscal 2028. They see free cash flow falling by more than half in fiscal 2027 and then recovering only partway:

Microsoft (MSFT): free cash flow, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2024-2028 (years to June) (TIKR)

Capex explains the drop. Microsoft's cash capital spending rose to $115.9 billion in fiscal 2026 from $64.6 billion, and analysts expect $193.7 billion in fiscal 2027.

Amazon was worth about $2.67 trillion, or about 75x the $35.7 billion of free cash flow analysts expect in 2028. To get there, it first goes through two years of negative free cash flow:

Amazon (AMZN): free cash flow, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2024-2028 (TIKR)

Its capex rose to $132 billion in 2025 from $52.7 billion in 2023:

Amazon (AMZN): capital expenditures, $ billions, fiscal 2021-2025 (TIKR)

Jassy's $220 billion for this year is roughly 1.7x that.

What the capex has to return

Say you'd pay 30x free cash flow, still a premium price. At Nov. 20 values, Microsoft would need about $120 billion a year, about 1.6x the $74.1 billion it made in fiscal 2024, its best year on the chart. Amazon would need about $89 billion a year, roughly 2.3x its 2024 figure of $38.2 billion. Neither has ever come close.

title: Bank of America doubles down on Amazon stock ahead of 2027
detail:
Bank of America doubles down on Amazon stock ahead of 2027
Hillary Remy, Aparajita Chatterjee
Sat, November 21, 2026 at 10:07 AM CST 5 min read
AMZN
UPS
FDX
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Amazon built the largest parcel delivery network in the United States without most investors paying close attention. The company went from a shipping customer dependent on UPS and FedEx to their biggest direct competitor in roughly a decade. That transition is now entering its next phase.

Bank of America analyst Justin Post brought in one of the most closely followed logistics researchers in the industry to make the case. The choice to bring in an outside expert signals conviction. Post did not build this argument on internal modeling alone.

Also read: Bank of America sends SpaceX stock investors strong signal

Post maintains a Buy rating on Amazon (AMZN) with a price target of $317, against a Nov. 17 closing price of $257.89. In a note shared with TheStreet, he detailed what logistics research firm MWPVL International sees when it examines Amazon's fulfillment network, automation roadmap, and delivery cost trajectory.

What Amazon's 2027 capacity buildout actually looks like

The logistics network is closer to full than the stock price suggests. MWPVL International principal Marc Wulfraat presented to Bank of America on where things stand, and his read, cited in the note shared with TheStreet, is that the response to that pressure will be significantly larger in 2027.

Amazon is expected to add approximately 91 million gross square feet of fulfillment and delivery space next year, up 38% from roughly 66 million square feet in 2026.

The capital behind that expansion runs at approximately $28 billion across 2026 and 2027 for new supply chain facilities, excluding maintenance and retrofits. That figure could rise by $10 billion on an annualized basis.

The planned spend will focus on small, sortable robotic fulfillment centers, inbound cross-dock facilities, and delivery stations. Post noted that the retail figure remains modest compared with his estimate of $240 billion in AWS capital expenditure in 2027.

Amazon's delivery network runs 592 stations in the United States today. MWPVL projects expansion toward approximately 950 by 2030. Amazon expects to move approximately 8 billion packages in 2026, up from 6 billion in 2024, and that volume is running ahead of what the existing infrastructure was sized for.

Gen14 centers and what the next generation of automation changes

The automation story has two chapters, and neither has arrived yet. Amazon's Gen14 fulfillment centers are expected to open in 2028, with seven sites already in the pipeline. These centers are more compact than what the company operates today, designed for smaller sortable items and with significantly less square footage than Gen11 and Gen12 facilities.

Jim Cramer: Amazon Could Sell Its Anthropic Stake and Say "Our CapEx Is Paid For." Does the Math Work? © Viktoryia Vinnikava's Images and Tiger Lily from Pexels via Canva
Key Takeaways

Jim Cramer said Amazon could sell its Anthropic stake and have its capex "paid for for the next year and a half."

The Anthropic shares Amazon owns outright were worth about $188 billion at the first-day close, about 10 months of this year's capex.

Amazon only needs to cover its free cash flow shortfall, about $65 billion across 2026 and 2027, and those shares cover it more than twice over.

Andy Jassy says Amazon will hold the stake. It's a backstop, and its value, like Salesforce's, now moves with Anthropic's stock.

Anthropic's IPO made Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ) one of the market's biggest winners on paper, and Jim Cramer has an idea for what to do with the winnings.

Anthropic (ANT:NASDAQ) closed its first day of trading Thursday at $97.17, 17% above its $83 IPO price, then fell 8.5% to $88.91 on Friday as AI stocks sold off. On Squawk on the Street, CNBC's Cramer laid out the math:

"that number of their ownership in Anthropic is more than equivalent to what they're going to spend in CapEx. They could actually sell the stake and say, hey, our CapEx is paid for for the next year and a half."

That would be quite the trick. CEO Andy Jassy told CNBC's Halftime Report on Nov. 17 that "we expect to spend around $220 billion this year in CapEx and that we expect to spend meaningfully more next year."

Free cash flow has gone negative

That spending has already pushed Amazon's free cash flow below zero. Analysts don't expect it to turn positive again until 2028:

Amazon (AMZN): free cash flow, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2023-2028 (TIKR)

So far, Amazon has filled the gap mostly by borrowing. Its long-term debt rose from $65.6 billion at the end of 2025 to $173.1 billion at Sept. 30, more than doubling in nine months.

TIKR tracks 62 analysts on Amazon. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Amazon, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Amazon's Analyst Ratings

Cramer counts the notes

After the IPO, Amazon owns 14.6% of Anthropic outright. At the first-day close, those shares were worth about $188 billion, roughly 10 months of this year's capex.

Cramer's figure is 23.6%, because it also counts convertible notes Amazon hasn't converted, held back under an ownership cap it has chosen not to waive. At the $1.5 trillion valuation he used, that's about $354 billion, or about 19 months of spending at this year's pace.

But Amazon's capex has more than doubled in five years:

Amazon (AMZN): capital expenditures, $ billions, fiscal 2021-2025 (TIKR)

Analysts expect $278.2 billion in 2027, and at that pace even Cramer's $354 billion covers only about 15 months.

Anthropic Owes $71 Billion for Compute Within a Year, "87% of Current Run Rate Revenue," per Scott Galloway ©jiefeng jiang from Getty Images and Quality Stock Arts via Canva
Key Takeaways

Scott Galloway says $71 billion of Anthropic's compute commitments come due within a year, a bill that reaches Amazon, Alphabet and Broadcom.

With over $200 billion of cash after its IPO, Anthropic can pay it, so the bigger worry is its slowing revenue growth.

Galloway says compute costs nearly doubled in the third quarter, and TIKR's figures put Anthropic's operating margin at minus 3.3%.

Anthropic's first report as a public company will show whether growth can reach analysts' $128 billion revenue estimate for 2027.

Anthropic (ANT:NASDAQ) closed its first day of trading, November 19, at $97.17, 17% above its $83 IPO price. On November 20 it gave some of that back, falling 8.5% to $88.91 in a broad sell-off of AI and chip stocks, as investors weighed what its numbers can carry. That question matters to Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ), Alphabet (GOOG) and Broadcom (AVGO:NASDAQ) too.

On the November 20 episode of Pivot, NYU Stern professor Scott Galloway pointed to Anthropic's compute commitments, which he put at $900 billion through 2045. Then came the part that's due soon:

"71 billion comes due of that commitment in the next 12 months or about 87% of current run rate revenue."

Which, yikes.

Much of that bill lands as revenue at Amazon, Alphabet and Broadcom.

Revenue won't sit still for 12 months

But Anthropic's revenue is still climbing, if more slowly. By Galloway's count, "growth slowed in Q3 from 144% to 47%," quarter over quarter.

Prof G Markets co-host Ed Elson expects more of the same: "now it appears it's going to come down to between 15 to 25 percent."

Consensus is more optimistic, with revenue going from $54.4 billion in 2026 to $128 billion in 2027:

Anthropic, PBC (ANT): revenue, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2026-2028 (TIKR)

If Anthropic gets there, $71 billion is a bit over half of what it brings in during 2027. Still heavy, but a long way from 87%.

TIKR tracks 5 analysts on Anthropic. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Anthropic, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Anthropic's Analyst Ratings

Most of the compute goes to research

Anthropic CFO Krishna Rao told Bloomberg Talks on November 19 that the company ran an 85% gross margin and a 12% adjusted operating margin over the first nine months of 2026. On a GAAP basis, its amended S-1 puts that operating margin at minus 4%.

Both can be true, since Rao said Anthropic can "allocate the substantial majority of our compute fleet towards R&D," which sits below gross profit.
